items.prompt: What is a "role definition" in the sense this unit uses it?
choices: A concrete list of the specific skills, behaviors, or outcomes a hire genuinely needs to succeed in this role
The official job title listed on the offer letter
A general description of the company's culture and values
The salary band approved for the position
items.explanation: A role definition is specifically about the concrete requirements this job needs — not the title, culture, or compensation, which don't help design an interview loop.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, did the team appear to have a specific role definition before interviewing the candidate?
choices: No — the team's process suggests they were evaluating a general impression rather than testing against specific, predetermined signals
Yes — the role definition is what caused them to make the offer so quickly
Yes, and it explicitly excluded incident-diagnosis skills as a requirement
It's impossible to know whether a role definition existed from the Scenario's facts
items.explanation: The rushed, impression-based process and the resulting gap (an untested core skill) both point to the absence of a specific role definition driving the loop.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does defining the role before interviewing matter?
choices: It's what makes it possible to design a loop that deliberately tests for what the role needs, instead of hoping a good overall impression happens to cover them
It's a legal requirement in most hiring processes
It guarantees the team will make an offer faster
It removes the need for a debrief conversation afterward
items.explanation: L1 frames role definition as the thing that makes deliberate, targeted testing possible — not a speed shortcut or a compliance checkbox.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what would writing the role definition first have most directly enabled?
choices: Designing interview slots that individually test incident diagnosis, instead of repeating a general impression check
Making the offer to the candidate even faster than they already did
Skipping the interview process entirely
Guaranteeing the candidate would turn out to be a bad hire
items.explanation: A role definition written first is what lets a team point specific slots at specific requirements — exactly the step the Scenario's rushed process skipped.

items.prompt: How does a "signal" relate to a "role definition"?
choices: A signal is the observable evidence that a specific requirement from the role definition was actually demonstrated
A signal replaces the need for a role definition entirely
A signal is a synonym for the role definition — the two terms mean the same thing
A signal is only relevant after an offer has already been made
items.explanation: The role definition states what's required; a signal is the concrete, observed evidence that a specific requirement was actually met.

items.prompt: If a role definition lists "can explain a trade-off clearly to a non-technical stakeholder," what would count as a signal for it?
choices: A candidate actually explaining a trade-off clearly to a non-technical stakeholder during an interview exercise
The candidate stating on their resume that they're a good communicator
The interviewer's general feeling that the candidate seemed articulate
A reference confirming the candidate is friendly
items.explanation: A signal has to be a direct, observed demonstration of the specific requirement — not a self-report, a vague impression, or an unrelated trait.

items.prompt: What is a "signal" in this unit's hiring framework?
choices: A specific, observable piece of evidence that a role definition's requirement was actually demonstrated
A red flag that automatically disqualifies a candidate
The overall gut feeling an interviewer has about a candidate
A reference check from a candidate's previous employer
items.explanation: A signal is concrete, checkable evidence tied to a specific requirement — not a general impression, a disqualifier, or a reference call.

items.prompt: Which of these is closer to a genuine "signal" as this unit defines it?
choices: The candidate correctly diagnosed the root cause in a live incident-diagnosis exercise
The candidate seemed very confident throughout the interview
The candidate has five years of experience listed on their resume
The interviewer had a good feeling about the candidate
items.explanation: A specific, demonstrated action tied to a defined requirement is a signal — general confidence, years of experience, or a vague feeling are not the same as observed evidence.

items.prompt: What is the "halo effect"?
choices: The tendency for one salient positive trait to bias the perceived strength of other, unrelated traits
The tendency for interviewers to favor candidates who are late to the interview
A scoring bonus given to internal referrals
The tendency for a candidate's skills to improve during the interview process
items.explanation: The halo effect is specifically about one trait unconsciously coloring judgment of unrelated traits — not about lateness, referrals, or actual skill improvement.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, which trait most plausibly triggered a halo effect across the panel?
choices: The candidate's confidence and articulateness
The candidate's specific incident-diagnosis skill, which was never tested
The candidate's years of prior experience
The candidate's salary expectations
items.explanation: Confidence and articulateness are the visible, salient traits described in the Scenario — the untested skill (incident diagnosis) is exactly what the halo effect caused the panel to assume without checking.

items.prompt: What distinguishes a "structured interview loop" from an unstructured one?
choices: Each interview slot is assigned to test a specific, predetermined signal, and interviewers score independently before comparing notes
A structured loop always has more interview slots than an unstructured one
A structured loop is conducted entirely over video calls instead of in person
A structured loop always takes place over multiple days instead of one
items.explanation: Structure is about what each slot deliberately tests and independent scoring — not about the number of slots, the medium, or the schedule.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, was the loop that actually ran structured in this sense?
choices: No — the interviews appear to have been open-ended conversations rather than each slot targeting a distinct, predetermined signal
Yes — each interviewer was assigned a distinct signal and scored independently
Yes, but only the final debrief step was structured
It's impossible to tell whether the loop was structured from the Scenario's facts
items.explanation: The Scenario describes interviewers coming away with a general positive impression, not independent evidence against distinct signals — the hallmark of an unstructured loop.

items.prompt: Why did every interviewer in the Scenario come away impressed, while the actual core skill went untested?
choices: All the interviewers were likely reacting to the same salient trait (confidence) rather than each testing something different
The interviewers were specifically instructed not to test technical skills
The candidate lied about their skills during the interview
The interviewers didn't have enough time to form any impression at all
items.explanation: Five people agreeing isn't five independent data points if they were all responding to the same visible trait rather than testing distinct signals.

items.prompt: What was the immediate trigger for skipping part of the Scenario's planned interview loop?
choices: Being understaffed and wanting to close the hiring gap quickly
The candidate refused to continue the interview process
The remaining interviewer was unavailable for the rest of the year
The role definition explicitly said the technical interview was optional
items.explanation: The Scenario describes urgency from being short-staffed as the reason the technical deep-dive was cut, not any issue with the candidate or a documented decision to skip it.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, if five interviewers all rate a candidate highly based on the same salient trait, how many independent data points does that actually represent?
choices: Effectively one — all five ratings trace back to the same single trait, not five separately-tested skills
Five — agreement across five interviewers always means five independent data points
Zero — agreement across interviewers is never meaningful
It depends only on how confident the candidate was, not on what was actually tested
items.explanation: L2's diagram shows every interviewer's positive impression tracing back to the same source trait — that's one signal repeated, not five independent ones.

items.prompt: Per L2, is confidence or charisma in a candidate inherently a problem?
choices: No — the problem is confidence becoming a proxy for unrelated, untested traits, not confidence itself
Yes — confident candidates should always be rated lower to counteract bias
Yes — charisma is never a legitimate signal for any role
No, but only for technical roles specifically
items.explanation: L2 explicitly clarifies the issue isn't the trait itself, but treating it as a stand-in for skills that were never actually, independently tested.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, why is "a strong engineer" not specific enough to interview against, while "can independently diagnose a production incident from partial information" is?
choices: The second is a checkable, observable signal an interviewer can design an exercise around; the first is a vague trait with no clear test
The second is shorter and therefore easier to remember during an interview
The first describes a trait no candidate could ever demonstrate
There's no real difference — both are equally specific for interview purposes
items.explanation: Specificity is what makes a requirement testable — a vague adjective gives an interviewer nothing concrete to design an exercise around.

items.prompt: Does L2's example table claim that every role needs the same three signals it lists?
choices: No — the point is that whatever signals a specific role actually needs should be written down and specific, not that this exact list is universal
Yes — every role, regardless of function, should test for all three exact signals listed
No — the table's signals only ever apply to engineering roles
Yes, but only the communication signal is universally required
items.explanation: L2 explicitly states a different role would need a different, equally specific list — the table illustrates the pattern, not a universal checklist.

items.prompt: Per L2, once signals are defined, what changes about how each interview slot is used?
choices: Each slot gets assigned to test one specific signal, and interviewers score independently before comparing notes with each other
Every slot becomes a general open-ended conversation, just longer
Interview slots are removed entirely in favor of a single written test
Each slot is assigned to test all the signals at once
items.explanation: The core design move is mapping distinct signals to distinct slots with independent scoring — not lengthening or eliminating conversations.

items.prompt: Why does independent scoring before comparing notes matter, per L2?
choices: If an interviewer's assessment is shared before others form their own, it can anchor the rest of the panel's scores regardless of what they actually observed
It matters only for legal compliance reasons, not for assessment accuracy
It doesn't matter — comparing notes early always improves accuracy
It matters only when the panel has more than five interviewers
items.explanation: Early sharing risks anchoring the rest of the panel to one person's impression, defeating the purpose of having independently-tested signals in the first place.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of running every interview as an open-ended conversation?
choices: Every interviewer ends up measuring roughly the same thing — usually likability — providing far less real coverage than the number of interviews suggests
Open-ended conversations always produce lower overall candidate ratings
Open-ended conversations take less total time than structured ones
There's no real risk — open-ended conversations are equivalent to structured ones
items.explanation: Without each slot targeting something distinct, multiple interviews collapse into repeated measurements of the same general impression rather than genuine, broad coverage.

items.prompt: Per L2, is "everyone on the panel liked them" equivalent to "we tested everything the role needs"?
choices: No — agreement across the panel only means something if each interviewer was actually testing something different
Yes — unanimous positive feedback always means full coverage of the role's requirements
Yes, but only if the panel has at least four interviewers
No, but only because panels are inherently unreliable regardless of structure
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns against treating consensus as proof of coverage — consensus is only meaningful when it comes from independently-tested, distinct signals.

items.prompt: Per L2, what actually determines what each interview slot tests?
choices: The specific signals identified in the role definition — the loop is designed around them, not the other way around
Whichever topics the interviewer personally finds most interesting
The order candidates are scheduled to interview in
The candidate's resume, which sets the agenda for each slot
items.explanation: L2's loop-design section is explicit: signals come from the role definition first, and slots get built around them — not the reverse.

items.prompt: Per L2, could a team design its interview slots first and figure out the role definition afterward?
choices: No — the role definition needs to exist first so the loop can be deliberately mapped to it, not guessed at afterward
Yes — the order makes no difference to the loop's quality
Yes, as long as the debrief happens before the role definition is written
No, but only because most companies require it for legal reasons
items.explanation: The whole mechanism L2 describes — assigning each slot a specific signal — depends on the signals already being defined; there's nothing to map slots to otherwise.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, why is "can independently diagnose a production incident from partial, ambiguous information" usable in an interview while "technically strong" is not?
choices: The first is something a candidate can actually be observed doing in a designed exercise; the second gives no clear task to test
The first is a shorter phrase and therefore easier for interviewers to remember
The second describes a trait no candidate could ever have
There's no real difference — both are equally usable in an interview
items.explanation: Specificity is what makes a requirement testable — a vague adjective gives an interviewer nothing concrete to build an exercise around.

items.prompt: Per L2's framing, which of these could an interviewer actually design a 45-minute exercise around?
choices: Identify which of three proposed fixes for a bug addresses the root cause, not just the symptom
Seems technically strong overall
Has good judgment in general
Comes across as a strong communicator
items.explanation: A concrete, checkable task can be turned directly into an exercise; a general adjective can't — that's exactly the distinction L2's table draws.

items.prompt: In L3's five-slot comparison table, which slots did the Scenario's actual loop cut, and what did that cost?
choices: The stakeholder-communication and code-review exercises — both of the slots most likely to test signals beyond the general impression already formed
The initial rapport-building conversation — the least important slot in either version of the loop
The debrief step — meaning no discussion happened at all after interviews
None of the slots were cut; the Scenario's loop matched the structured version exactly
items.explanation: L3's table shows interviews 3 and 4 (mapped to stakeholder communication and code review) were the ones cut for speed — along with, separately, incident diagnosis never being properly tested either.

items.prompt: Per L3, does a structured loop necessarily require more total interview slots than an unstructured one?
choices: No — it takes the same number of slots, deliberately pointed at different, specific signals instead of repeating the same general impression
Yes — structured loops always require at least twice as many interviews
Yes, because independent scoring requires a dedicated extra slot
No — structured loops always require fewer total interviews than unstructured ones
items.explanation: L3 explicitly notes the slot count doesn't need to change — what changes is what each slot is deliberately testing.

items.prompt: Per L3, what would a properly structured debrief report have looked like for the incident-diagnosis interview, versus what actually happened?
choices: A specific, falsifiable observation (which cause was picked, and whether the others were correctly ruled out) instead of a vague "I thought they were great overall"
An anonymous numeric score with no accompanying explanation at all
A recommendation on salary and start date, with no assessment of skills
Identical to what actually happened — L3 shows the debrief content wouldn't have changed either way
items.explanation: The value of a structured slot is a concrete, checkable observation the hiring manager can actually weigh — not a repeat of the same vague positive impression.

items.prompt: Per L3, does catching the incident-diagnosis gap in the loop guarantee the team wouldn't still hire this candidate?
choices: No — the team might still make the offer, but with a clear plan (like an onboarding focus) instead of an unpleasant surprise three months in
Yes — any gap found during a structured loop automatically disqualifies a candidate
Yes, because structured loops are designed to always reject candidates with any weakness
No, but only because structured loops are legally required to result in an offer
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the loop's value isn't guaranteeing a different outcome — it's making sure whatever decision is made is based on what was actually demonstrated.

items.prompt: Per L3's "what generalizes" section, does the halo-effect risk from this hiring example apply only to engineering interview panels?
choices: No — it generalizes to any panel-based evaluation, including promotion committees, vendor selection panels, and grant review boards
Yes — the halo effect is specific to technical hiring and doesn't apply to other panel contexts
No, but only to panels with more than ten members
Yes, but only when the panel is evaluating candidates under time pressure
items.explanation: L3 explicitly extends the core lesson (agreement is only meaningful if it comes from independent, distinct testing) to any panel-based evaluation, not just engineering hiring.

items.prompt: Per L3, if the team were hiring a technical writer instead of an engineer, should they reuse the exact same three signals from the Scenario's role definition?
choices: No — a different role needs its own, equally specific list of signals, not the engineering-specific list reused
Yes — the same three signals apply equally well to any role in the company
Yes, but only the code-review signal should be swapped out
No — technical writer roles don't need a role definition at all
items.explanation: L3 explicitly frames the three signals as specific to this engineering role — a different role needs its own specific, checkable list built the same way, not a copy-paste of this one.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes table, what's the risk of writing a role definition once and never revisiting it?
choices: A stale role definition tests for what used to matter, not what the role currently requires, as the team or product changes
Nothing — a role definition is accurate forever once it's written
It becomes illegal to use in a hiring process after a fixed period
Candidates will always notice and refuse to interview
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that a role's real requirements shift over time — a role definition written once and left alone drifts out of sync with what actually matters now.

items.prompt: Per L3, should a role definition be treated as a one-time document?
choices: No — it should be revisited as the role's actual requirements shift
Yes — revisiting it would make interview scoring inconsistent across candidates
Yes, because signals never change once a role exists
No, but only for engineering roles specifically
items.explanation: L3 lists "writing a role definition once and never revisiting it" as its own named failure mode — the fix is treating it as a living document, not a one-off artifact.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's wrong with treating a structured loop as bureaucracy to cut under time pressure?
choices: It defeats the loop's actual purpose — catching exactly the kind of gap the Scenario's rushed hire hit
Nothing — a structured loop only exists to slow down hiring managers
It's wrong only when the company is hiring for a senior role
It's wrong only if the candidate complains about the process
items.explanation: L3 frames the structured loop as risk management, not overhead — cutting it under pressure is exactly what let the Scenario's gap through undetected.

items.prompt: Per L3, is cutting a loop step under time pressure inherently wrong?
choices: Not inherently — but it should be a deliberate trade-off against a known, specific signal, not a generic "we've seen enough"
Yes — no loop step should ever be cut, regardless of circumstances
No — cutting steps is always the right call when a team is short-staffed
Yes, but only because it violates a company policy L3 describes
items.explanation: L3's failure mode is specifically about cutting a step without checking what signal is lost — a deliberate, informed trade-off is a different thing entirely.

items.prompt: Per L3, what makes "given a partial log with three plausible causes, they picked the most likely one but couldn't explain why the other two were less likely" a better debrief report than "I thought they were great overall"?
choices: It's a specific, falsifiable observation the hiring manager can actually weigh, not a vague overall impression
It's shorter and therefore faster to read in a debrief meeting
It uses more technical vocabulary, which always signals rigor
There's no real difference — both convey the same information
items.explanation: The value L3 highlights is concreteness and falsifiability — a specific claim about what was and wasn't demonstrated, not a restated positive vibe.

items.prompt: Per L3, what is the hiring manager able to do with a specific debrief observation that they can't do with a vague one?
choices: Weigh the concrete gap against how urgently the seat needs filling, and decide with eyes open
Automatically reject the candidate without further discussion
Skip the rest of the hiring loop for the next candidate
Avoid ever making a hiring decision under uncertainty
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the loop's value isn't guaranteeing a particular outcome — it's making sure the eventual decision is based on a real, weighable observation.
